cues.text: Welcome to Strategic Resilience Intelligence. This tutorial will walk through the tool at a comfortable pace.
Its purpose is to explore how maintenance choices, sustainability questions, and operational resilience can be assessed together.
This is a decision-support prototype. It does not measure fleet readiness or make approved Airbus operational decisions.
Notice the four steps: Investigate, Challenge, Check, and Translate. We will work through all four.
In Investigate, a fictional aerospace test bench loses an electronic control module. We need to restore a working module.
The deadline is sixty days. Buying a replacement carries a long supplier lead time and a risk of additional disruption.
The repair option has a seventy-five percent feasibility assumption. These are invented numbers, not observed Airbus data.
We can buy new, attempt repair first, or launch both routes. Each has different implications for time, money, and resources.
Click Make a decision to enter the interactive comparison. The scenario is the same; now we choose a response.
At the top of Challenge, the scenario selector controls the background assumptions. It is not the strategy selector.
Other presets simulate disruptions, cost pressure, low repair feasibility, or correlated risks. We will use the starting case.
Below are three strategy cards. They answer a different question: what should the team do in this scenario?
First, choose a new component. This means placing a replacement order and accepting supplier lead times.
The result panel calculates expected recovery time, the chance of meeting sixty days, and expected cash spending.
Now choose the parallel strategy. It starts procurement and repair together, potentially gaining speed at extra cost.
Parallel action can reduce exposure to a single failure route, but cancellation obligations and duplicate work still matter.
Finally, select Repair First. This is the route we will analyse in detail and carry through the tutorial.
The initial average recovery time is fifty days. That number is not the time spent physically repairing the component.
The next indicator is the probability of getting an operational module within sixty days. It is not a guarantee.
The third indicator estimates cash outlay. The three metrics together reveal trade-offs rather than one universal winner.
Open the explanation beneath the metrics. If repair succeeds, recovery is quicker. If it fails, replacement follows.
The comparison text explains how the selected strategy differs from the other two on timing, spending, and deadline risk.
Notice the warning: modelled outcomes depend on the inputs. They cannot be presented as demonstrated Airbus benefits.
Select Change Conditions. This is where the tool becomes interactive rather than simply displaying a result.
The basic controls include repair feasibility, repair duration, replacement lead time, supplier risk, and the target date.
Here, repair feasibility starts at seventy-five percent. The model treats this as a probability, not a certification.
Change the feasibility assumption from seventy-five to ninety percent. Watch the result update immediately.
Expected average recovery falls from fifty to thirty-six point eight days. The other indicators also recalculate.
Why? A quicker successful repair now receives more weight in the average, and the slower fallback becomes less likely.
Changing supplier lead time or disruption probability can reverse the trade-off. We should test assumptions, not cherry-pick results.
Open the advanced inputs. Inspection time, extra supplier delays, and dependence between risks can also be specified.
The Costs section includes inspection, repair, purchase, logistics, and disruption charges. These are illustrative inputs.
The Contract section records what happens when one route wins: cancellation charges, commitments, and inventory treatment.
Environmental inputs cover materials, waste, and partial emissions. The model is explicit about its boundaries and uncertainty.
Return to the comparison. Our selected Repair First strategy remains visible, now under the changed assumption.
Now open View Analysis. This optional technical workspace lets us inspect how the headline metrics were calculated.
The first tab is Selected route breakdown. Each row represents a possible outcome under the strategy we chose.
Notice the branch probabilities. Repair success or failure is combined with possible supplier disruption.
Recovery time and financial obligations are calculated for each branch, then weighted to obtain the average.
The second tab asks when repair or replacement makes sense. It explores sensitivity rather than assuming fixed conditions.
The graph shows how an outcome changes when one input changes. It helps identify assumptions that drive the decision.
Selectors above the graph let us choose the input and the metric. These are hypothetical curves, not measured trends.
The decision boundaries below the graph indicate where routes may become comparable on time or spending.
Next is Environmental Effects. This is important, because avoiding a new purchase might reduce material demand.
The analysis considers materials, generated waste, and bounded greenhouse gas estimates compared with new procurement.
But none of those calculated environmental values is a verified benefit. The physical and data boundaries must be confirmed.
The Method and Equations tab explains the probability-weighted model, definitions, and calculation assumptions.
That transparency is essential: a credible resilience argument needs a reproducible mechanism, not a green headline.
Now we have both an operational comparison and an explanation of its limitations. Next we check the evidence.
Select Check. This step separates what the model predicts from what the available evidence actually supports.
A mathematically consistent result is not automatically proof of a business, environmental, or operational benefit.
The first evidence category contains documented information. Here we can identify the source behind a statement.
The second is an assumption still to be verified, such as whether a particular repair is technically approved.
The third is a model output. The recovery time and spending estimates result from invented inputs.
The conclusions section makes a critical distinction: what we can say today, and what remains to be demonstrated.
Engineering would need to confirm repair eligibility, duration, quality requirements, and additional approved service life.
Procurement would confirm actual delivery times, prices, supply disruption risks, and contract cancellation terms.
Environment would check the material, waste, and emissions data and define an honest comparison boundary.
Programme teams would decide whether component-level recovery translates into a measurable operational effect.
Open the optional technical documentation. It provides source references, evidence records, and validation criteria.
This evidence review protects the project from overstated claims. Only supported conclusions should be communicated.
Choose Translate, the fourth step. Here the same analytical result is expressed for different decision audiences.
The audience cards include Defence Customer, Programme Manager, Engineering, and Executive Leadership.
Select Engineering. The message now emphasises technical eligibility, underlying mechanisms, and proof still required.
The tool does not change the data when we change the audience. It changes the explanation and questions to be answered.
Now select Executive Leadership. This view focuses on strategic options, vulnerability, and the readiness of claims.
Resilience is not presented as a slogan: the summary links a decision to a specified risk and a conditional outcome.
The strategy cards also allow us to translate the results for replacement, repair first, or parallel response.
The principal conclusion and recommendation are modelled statements. Their status depends on the supporting evidence.
Further down, the three-way comparison describes the trade-offs and a decision test, rather than declaring a winner.
The Strategy Profile tab separates modelled advantages, drawbacks, and uncertainties for the selected route.
Causal Reasoning follows a chain from a sustainability initiative to environmental mechanisms and resilience outcomes.
Each link can be inspected. This is where we distinguish plausible pathways from benefits actually demonstrated.
Evidence Trace links individual statements to evidence identifiers and model outputs, making the narrative auditable.
The Validation Plan assigns the remaining checks to the relevant owners before anyone makes stronger claims.
Method and Limitations offers additional context. An uncertainty should remain visible even in an executive presentation.
Finally, open Review and Export. This is where the analysis becomes a shareable decision report.
The report shows the audience, selected strategy, scenario, result, and the scope of conclusions.
Automatic file checks do not validate the underlying facts. The prototype clearly marks unverified claims.
Before downloading, acknowledge that the conclusions depend on the quality and validation of the inputs.
The PDF is intended for reading and discussion. It includes conclusions, sources, limitations, and the analysis.
The JSON preserves structured inputs and calculations for reproducibility. This is useful for technical review.
That is the complete decision journey: investigate, compare, test conditions, verify evidence, and communicate responsibly.
